# Parallel and Background Agents

Last verified: 2026-10-29 against git-scm.com git-worktree, the Claude Code docs (worktrees, agent-view, sub-agents, overview, security), Cursor Cloud Agent docs and GitHub Copilot docs (see Sources). The git demo was re-run on macOS on 2026-10-29 by an independent checker.

Starts from: lesson 2 (task specs) and lesson 3 (repo setup for agents).
Builds on: engineering-rigor-at-speed lesson 3 (small diffs; review is the bottleneck).

## The problem and why it matters

You have five small tasks: two bug fixes, a docs update, a dependency bump, a test backfill. An agent (a program where a model reads files and runs commands in a loop) can do one in about the time it takes you to get coffee. So you start five at once in the same folder.

Within minutes, two agents have edited `utils.py`, one has run `git checkout` under another's feet, and the test run is red for reasons nobody can name. Parallelism without isolation is just a race condition (two actors changing the same thing, result depends on timing) with extra steps.

The other trap is quieter. You do isolate them, five clean branches appear, and now you owe five careful reviews. Starting work got cheap. Reading it did not. This lesson is about getting the isolation right and about knowing where the real cap is.

## First principles

1. **Isolate before you parallelize.** Each agent needs its own copy of the files and its own branch.
2. **Split by files, not by topic.** Two tasks that touch the same file will conflict no matter how you label them.
3. **Merge conflicts are a planning problem.** Avoid them when you split the work; resolving them afterwards is the expensive path.
4. **Coordination has a cost.** Every extra agent adds splitting, briefing, merging and checking that you do.
5. **Review bandwidth is the cap.** The number of agents you can use well equals the number of diffs you can review carefully (my experience, not a measured result).
6. **Isolation of files is not isolation of side effects.** Two agents can still hit the same database, port or API.

## How it works

### Four ways to run more than one agent

| Way | What is separate | What is shared |
|---|---|---|
| Subagents | Context window | Same session, same files |
| Worktrees | Files and branch | Git history, your machine |
| Background sessions | Your attention | Depends on isolation used |
| Cloud agents | Machine and files | Only the repo, via a pull request (PR) |

- **Subagent:** a helper inside one session that works in its own context window and returns a summary. It splits up thinking, not files.
- **Worktree:** a second working directory for the same repository, on its own branch.
- **Background session:** an agent that keeps running without your terminal attached.
- **Cloud agent:** an agent running on someone else's machine (a VM), usually ending in a pull request (PR: a proposed change someone reviews before it merges).

Claude Code's worktree docs say the same split: worktrees "isolate file edits", subagents "split work up inside one session".

### What a git worktree is

A normal clone has one folder with one branch checked out. A **worktree** gives the same repository more folders, each with its own branch, sharing one history. The git docs: a repository "can support multiple working trees, allowing you to check out more than one branch at a time." They share everything "except per-worktree files such as `HEAD`, `index`".

```
 project/            main  <- you
 project-a/          agent/a   <- agent 1
 project-b/          agent/b   <- agent 2
        \             |             /
         '--- one shared .git ------'
              (history, branches)
```

It is cheaper than three clones (one history) and safer than one folder (no stepping on each other's files).

### Runnable demo: worktrees, a clean merge and a conflict

Run on macOS with git 2.50.1 (Apple Git-155), 2026-10-29, in a throwaway directory. It builds a tiny repo, makes two agent worktrees, then shows three outcomes: a refusal, a clean merge and a conflict. Commit hashes differ on every run.

```bash
git init -q -b main app && cd app
printf 'def greet():\n    return "hi"\n' > util.py
printf 'def total():\n    return 0\n'     > billing.py
git add . && git commit -q -m "base"

git worktree add -q ../app-a -b agent/a
git worktree add -q ../app-b -b agent/b
git worktree list
git worktree add ../app-c agent/a        # same branch twice
```

Output:

```text
<repo>    d2b3589 [main]
<repo>-a  d2b3589 [agent/a]
<repo>-b  d2b3589 [agent/b]
Preparing worktree (checking out 'agent/a')
fatal: 'agent/a' is already used by worktree at '<tmp>/app-a'
```

Git refuses to put one branch in two folders. That is a free safety net: two agents cannot share a branch by accident.

Now each agent edits a different file and commits (`cd ../app-a`, change `billing.py`, commit; `cd ../app-b`, change `util.py`, commit). Back in `app`, merging both:

```text
both merged, no conflict
```

Different files, no conflict. Now both agents change the *same line* of `util.py` (one writes `"hey"`, the other `"yo"`), and we merge both into `main`:

```text
a2 merged
Auto-merging util.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in util.py
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
UU util.py
```

`UU` means both sides modified the file. Git cannot guess which greeting is right; a human or a third agent must decide, and either choice is a judgment about behavior. Clean up:

```bash
git merge --abort
git worktree remove ../app-a && git worktree remove ../app-b
git worktree list
```

```text
<repo>  bb2428e [main]
```

Note: `git worktree remove` only removes clean worktrees; commit or discard first (`--force` overrides). The `agent/a` and `agent/b` branches remain until you delete them.

What the demo shows: isolation is easy; the conflict is decided by how you split the work.

### Claude Code's built-in support (as of 2026-10-29)

From its docs; check them, because this area changes quickly.

```bash
claude --worktree feature-auth     # or -w
```

- Creates the worktree under `.claude/worktrees/<name>/` on a new branch `worktree-<name>`. The docs suggest adding `.claude/worktrees/` to `.gitignore`.
- A worktree is a fresh checkout, so install dependencies there. A `.worktreeinclude` file (`.gitignore` syntax) copies gitignored files such as `.env` into new worktrees. That copies secrets, so keep it short.
- On exit, a clean unnamed worktree is removed automatically; a clean named one prompts you first; one with work in it prompts you to keep or remove it.
- A subagent can get its own worktree via `isolation: worktree` in its frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the subagent's Markdown file). Worktrees branch from the default branch unless `worktree.baseRef` is set to `"head"`.
- Isolation checks block edits that target the main checkout, but the docs say a shell command such as `cp` writing into it is not caught by them. Permissions and sandboxing still apply.
- **Background sessions:** `claude --bg "prompt"` starts one; `claude agents` shows them all. Before editing, Claude moves the session into a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/`, with exceptions (for example a session you moved to the background after it was already editing). The page marks this as a research preview, says each session "uses your subscription quota independently", and that outside git, parallel sessions "aren't isolated from each other".
- It also notes that shutting down your machine stops running background sessions.

Cloud agents (Cursor Cloud Agents, GitHub's Copilot cloud agent, Claude Code on the web) run away from your laptop. Cursor's docs say its cloud agents "run in isolated VMs in the cloud" and "produce merge-ready PRs"; Claude Code's security page says each cloud session runs in an isolated, Anthropic-managed VM. Copilot's docs say it can only work on one branch at a time, and a branch protection rule "can prevent Copilot from creating or updating pull requests". My view, not a vendor claim: the upside is isolation from your laptop; the cost is that setup (dependencies, secrets, network) must be reproducible on their machine.

### Splitting work so it does not collide

```
 Task list
    |
    v
 which files does each touch?   (ask the agent
    |                            to LIST them
    v                            first, no edits)
 overlap?
   no  -> run in parallel
   yes -> sequence them, or merge the tasks
```

Rules of thumb (heuristics from my own practice):

- **Slice by module or directory**, never by "bug 1, bug 2".
- **Shared hot files** (lockfiles, route tables, `index.ts` barrels, generated code, migrations) get one owner. Put the dependency bump on its own, run alone.
- **Order matters for migrations.** Two agents each adding database migration number 12 will collide by name and by meaning.
- **Rebase early.** Merge `main` into an agent branch before it grows large; conflicts grow with age.
- **Say what not to touch** in the task: "Only edit files under `billing/`. Do not edit shared config."
- **Side effects collide even when files do not.** Two agents running integration tests against one local database, or both binding port 3000, will fail oddly. Give each its own port and test database, or run one at a time.

### Coordination limits

```
 agents:      1      3        6        10
 you spend:  write  write +   triage   mostly
             + read  read +   + merge  reviewing
                     merge
```

Each added agent shifts your time from writing to briefing, merging and reviewing. Past a point, you are a bottleneck with a long queue. A workable policy:

- Start at **two** parallel agents. Add a third only after both land clean.
- Cap by **open unreviewed diffs**, not by CPU. If three finished branches are waiting, start nothing new.
- Keep each task small enough to review in one sitting (engineering-rigor-at-speed lesson 3).
- Every agent must satisfy the same gate: tests, lint and the review checklist. Do not review less because there are more.

The best reason to parallelize is a *queue of independent, well-specified tasks with tests* (lesson 2). The worst is boredom while waiting for a single agent.

### Merging

```bash
git switch main
git merge --no-ff agent/a      # one at a time
# run the full test suite here, not only on the branch
git merge --no-ff agent/b
# run it again
```

Merge one branch at a time and test after each. Two branches can each pass alone and still break together (one renames a function, the other adds a call to the old name). That is a *semantic conflict*: no textual conflict, but broken behavior. Only tests catch it.

## Worked failure scenario

Three background agents are told: "update the logging calls", "add request IDs", "fix the timeout bug". All three merge cleanly. Production logs lose their request IDs.

1. **Symptom:** IDs missing only in the new endpoints.
2. **Cause:** agent 1 rewrote logging helpers (branch `a`); agent 2 added calls to the old helper (branch `b`). No text conflict; the merge was clean and tests did not cover log fields.
3. **Detect:** `git log --merges` and a diff of each branch against `main` showed both touched `logging/`.
4. **Fix:** a test that asserts a request ID appears in a log line; fix the call sites.
5. **Prevent:** the three tasks overlapped on one directory; they should have been sequenced. Add "list the files you will touch" to the task template.

(This scenario is constructed to show the pattern, not a recorded incident.)

## Common mistakes

- Parallel agents in one folder.
- Splitting by topic rather than by files.
- Starting more agents when finished branches are unreviewed.
- Merging all branches, then testing once.
- Forgetting that shared resources (database, port) are not isolated by worktrees.
- Copying `.env` secrets into every worktree and then leaving old worktrees around.
- Treating a cloud agent's PR as reviewed because it ran its own tests.

## Try it (15 minutes)

1. In a scratch repo, run the demo above. Confirm the refusal, the clean merge and the conflict.
2. Resolve the conflict by hand: edit `util.py`, `git add util.py`, `git commit`. Note that you had to decide the behavior.
3. Pick three real tasks from your backlog. For each, write the list of files it would touch. Mark any overlap.
4. Decide your cap: how many unreviewed diffs can you hold at once? Write the number at the top of your task list.
5. If you use Claude Code, try `claude --worktree try-it` and exit without changes. Per its docs, a clean worktree from a named session prompts you before removal (only an unnamed one is removed automatically), so answer "remove" and then check `git worktree list`.

## Checklist

1. Each agent has its own worktree and branch.
2. Tasks are split by files, and overlaps are sequenced.
3. Shared files and migrations have a single owner.
4. Ports, databases and APIs are not shared by accident.
5. I merge one branch at a time and test after each.
6. My cap is the number of diffs I can review, not agents I can start.
